title: The Revival, the heart's mirror
hookLine: the heart is a mirror, dulled by sins and polished by remembrance
tomorrow: bad news and good news in the same hour. now what?

cards: Step out of a hot shower and the bathroom mirror is a white blur. You can wipe a stripe with your hand and see one eye, then it fogs again. The Qur'an has a picture like that, only darker.
Of people who keep doing wrong, it says, in Pickthall's words: "Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts."
A hadith in at-Tirmidhi explains: each wrong leaves a dark spot on the heart, and turning back to God polishes it clean. So what fogs the mirror is what we do. What clears it?

teach.b: Al-Ghazali builds a whole picture on it in the Revival. The heart is a mirror, made to reflect what is true. Wrongdoing dulls it.

Remembrance of God, dhikr, polishes it, until it can show things as they really are. So far, everyone agrees. Here's where two teachers in this tradition lean different ways, and both deserve a hearing.
One view, which al-Ghazali presses in the Revival: remembrance polishes when the heart is in it.

teach.h: ONE VIEW: THE POLISH IS ATTENTION.
teach.b: Words on the tongue with a heart somewhere else do little; the polish is the attention.

teach.h: THE OTHER: DON'T PUT DOWN THE CLOTH.
teach.b: The other view, from Ibn Ata'illah, whose sayings arrive in a few days: don't give up remembrance because you don't feel present in it.

Forgetting God altogether is worse than remembering him distractedly, and remembering distractedly can lead to waking up, and waking up to presence. So keep saying the words; the heart may follow. Notice what they share.
Neither says the mirror is hopeless. Neither says to stop. One stresses where the polish comes from.
The other stresses not putting down the cloth.
And the surprising part, which both would sign: a fogged mirror isn't broken.
It's a mirror that needs wiping.

how: Muslims practice dhikr, repeating phrases such as subhanallah, alhamdulillah and astaghfirullah, often on prayer beads, and turn back to God after wrongdoing; Sufi teachers describe this as polishing the heart.

o: a book of dream meanings read by Muslims at night
a mosque's polished brass lamp hung near the prayer niche
al-Ghazali's great work, here picturing the heart as a mirror

games.q: the mirror and the two views — tap the pairs.

s: in this picture, a heart dulled by wrongdoing can't be cleaned
the hadith in at-Tirmidhi: turning back polishes it. fogged isn't broken.
Ibn Ata'illah says not to abandon remembrance even when you don't feel present
remembering distractedly can lead to waking up, and waking up to presence.
both teachers say to stop dhikr until your heart is fully in it
neither says stop. one stresses attention; the other, keeping going.

games.q: your friend says: just keep repeating the words, the heart follows on its own. she asks you for the best case for the other view. what do you give her?
o: dhikr is pointless unless you're perfectly focused, so don't bother.
the polish comes from the heart's attention; words with an absent heart do little, so aim for presence.
only scholars can polish the heart; ordinary people should just pray.
games.why: that's the strong form of al-Ghazali's view in the Revival. Ibn Ata'illah answers: don't put the words down while you wait for presence. both want the mirror clear.

practice: On each out-breath, say one word of remembrance softly: subhanallah, glory be to God. Some breaths your mind will be there and some it won't. Keep the cloth moving either way, one breath, one word, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The Revival, again: here the heart pictured as a mirror, dulled by wrongdoing and polished by remembrance.

orig.note: Arabic: dhikr, remembrance of God, which al-Ghazali says polishes the heart's mirror.

carryVoice: Hold this up today: the mirror. Fogged isn't broken, and wiping is allowed to take a while.

sources.q: Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts.
